In TCP/IP the network layer has more than one protocol. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is a support protocol for IP: the Internet's control messaging.

  • It reports errors at the network layer.
  • It reports unexpected events.
  • It reports information about the network, in response to queries.

It only reports the error: it does not specify what corrective action to take.

Its messages come in two families: error reports and query / reply.
IP delivers on a best-effort basis; ICMP tells what happened, but does not fix it.
An ICMP message goes inside an IP datagram

ICMP does not use TCP or UDP: it is encapsulated directly in IP, with its own protocol code, 1.

All messages start the same way:

  • Type and Code (8 bits each).
  • ICMP Checksum (16 bits).
  • The rest of the header, which changes depending on the message.
  • Data (0 to 68 bytes).
Protocol field of the IP header = 1 → what follows is an ICMP message.
In an echo, the rest of the header carries an identifier and a sequence number to match each request with its reply.

When it is impossible to deliver or forward a datagram, the router sends an ICMP message to the source before discarding it.

The message states the reason. The two most common:

  • Network unreachable: the router does not know how to reach the destination network.
  • Host unreachable: the destination network was reached, but the host cannot be found.

The other reasons are in the table. Here R2 has no route to the requested network.
The router discards it, but not silently: it tells the source why.

Each router decrements the TTL of the datagram before forwarding it. When a router detects that the TTL must become 0, the packet has reached the end of its life.

The router discards it and notifies the source with a time exceeded ICMP message.

In the example, A sends with TTL = 2: R1 lowers it to 1 and forwards it; R2 would lower it to 0, so it discards it and notifies.
The notice is signed: the source IP of the ICMP is that of the router that discarded the datagram.
The source receives a time exceeded ICMP sent by 200.69.225.150. Without meaning to, it has just learned which router is 2 hops away. This is what traceroute relies on.
Echo request, echo reply, and ping

With an echo request a source wants to know whether a destination is reachable. If the destination receives it, it answers with an echo reply that includes the same data as the request.

Ping is based on this exchange: it sends echo requests and shows the replies received, with the round-trip time of each.

In the example from the notes: 4 sent, 4 received, 0% loss, between 183 and 218 ms.
Ping = echo request going out + echo reply coming back. If it returns, there is a path in both directions.

The echo reply may not arrive for several reasons:

  • The request does not reach the destination.
  • A network administrator or a firewall blocks ICMP.
  • The destination's operating system deliberately does not answer ping.
  • The reply is lost on the way back.

Disabling all ICMP is not good practice: there are usually recommendations about which messages to let through and which not.
A ping that does not come back does not mean the destination cannot be reached.
a firewall or an administrator blocks ICMP
the destination OS does not answer ping
the reply is lost on the way

Traceroute is an application that tries to trace the path to a destination, showing each hop.

It starts by sending three echo requests with TTL = 1. The first router decrements the TTL, reaches 0, discards the packet, and returns a time exceeded. That way the router gets identified.

The first hop always shows the IP of the default gateway. It does this three times, which is why there are three times per line.
Traceroute deliberately triggers the TTL error so that each router gives itself away.

Next it sends three new requests with TTL = 2: they pass through the first hop, which decrements one, and die at the second router, which responds. Then TTL = 3, and so on iteratively, moving forward among the routers.

If * * * appears on a line, there was no error message: it is a router that does not want to respond.

It keeps advancing anyway: requests with a higher TTL go through it without problems and the following routers are discovered.
The asterisks do not break the trace: that router forwards packets, it just does not answer ICMP.
The destination responds with an echo reply

With enough TTL, the request no longer dies at any router: it reaches the destination.

The destination does not return a time exceeded but an echo reply. That is the signal that the end was reached: the trace is complete and it is known how many hops it took.

In the capture from the notes, www.yahoo.com appears at hop 12, and hops 6 and 7 show asterisks.
Time exceeded = still more path to go. Echo reply = you arrived.

• ICMP is IP's support protocol: it reports errors and events, it does not fix them. It travels in IP with protocol 1.
  • Destination unreachable: the router could neither deliver nor forward, and says why.
  • Time exceeded: the TTL reached 0.
  • Ping: echo request and echo reply.
  • Traceroute: TTL 1, 2, 3… until the echo reply is received; * * * is a router that does not answer.
